claims.text: At elevated temperatures, a stable, adherent oxide film is the dominant mechanism controlling the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
The multicomponent FeNiCrCoCu composition promotes formation of a protective oxide layer.
The oxide layer reduces direct metal-on-metal contact and thereby lowers wear.
The baseline coating is equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu deposited as a thin film on a steel substrate.
Near room temperature, the baseline coating develops only minimal oxide.
Changing the environment from inert gas to air while increasing temperature should alter oxide-scale development and wear behavior.
A cohesive, thermally grown oxide scale forms on the FeNiCrCoCu coating during high-temperature operation in air.
Oxidation in air is thermally activated and produces a protective scale that reduces frictional contact and mitigates wear.
Suppressing oxidation with an inert atmosphere causes wear to remain higher at elevated temperatures than in air.
In air at 500–800 °C, wear-volume loss should be at least 20–30% lower than under the room-temperature baseline condition.
In air at 500–800 °C, the coefficient of friction should be at least 20–30% lower than under the room-temperature baseline condition.
At 800 °C under atmospheric conditions, wear resistance can be greater than at lower temperatures.
Wear resistance does not improve monotonically from room temperature through 500 °C; wear depth may initially increase before decreasing at higher temperatures.
The proposed mechanism is applicable from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C under normal loads of 5–15 N.
The behavior above 800 °C or under extreme loading is uncertain.
Small composition differences and coating–substrate interactions may alter the nature, adherence, and protective effect of the oxide scale.
If elevated-temperature wear is reduced in air despite no significant oxide layer being present, oxide-scale formation is not the controlling explanation.
If oxidation-suppressed inert conditions produce wear as low as in air, the proposed oxide-controlled mechanism is falsified.
